original: The KJV’s Isaiah 6:9 and 6:10 are commands: the hearers are told to hear and not understand, and the prophet is told to make the heart of the people fat. The Greek New Testament prints at Acts 28:26–27 the same words as Brenton’s Greek of Isaiah for these clauses, and the KJV’s Acts 28:26–27 words them as statements. The KJV’s Isaiah and its Acts therefore word the same clauses differently.

original: Read in the KJV, the waters bring forth the moving creature and the fowl in chapter 1, while chapter 2 forms the fowl from the ground. Brenton’s Greek of 1:20 has one verb, “let the waters bring forth”, governing both the creeping creatures and the flying birds, so the Greek reads as the KJV does. The Hebrew has a verb for the waters (they swarm) whose object is the swarm of living creatures, and then a separate clause in which the fowl themselves fly. On the Hebrew wording, chapter 1 does not say what the fowl came from, and 2:19 says they were formed from the ground. The conflict therefore exists in the KJV and the Greek, and is not clearly present in the Hebrew.

original:
Preserved draft reasoning:
A heap is a pile of water standing up, and a wineskin is a bag that holds it. The KJV has the former. The Greek has ὡσεὶ ἀσκὸν. The Hebrew has כַּ֭נֵּד in that slot, and the KJV reading follows it. The two English pictures differ: waters piled up against a limit, or waters held inside a container.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
A heap is a pile of the waters standing on one another. A skin bottle is a vessel that holds them. The Greek ἀσκός is the word for a leather bag or wineskin, and Brenton’s English prints “bottle”. The two texts give two pictures of how the sea is gathered, as a mound in the KJV and as the contents of a container in the Greek.

The KJV states a vineyard; the Greek names no vineyard in this clause.

The Greek has two Greek nouns in that place, εἰδώλοις (idols) and ματαίοις (vain things). Neither text prints a word for evil spirits.

original: In the KJV the second item bought in Egypt beside horses is “linen yarn”, a commodity. original:
Preserved draft reasoning:
The Hebrew of 1 Chronicles 17:14 prints בְּבֵיתִי וּבְמַלְכוּתִי, “in my house, in my kingdom”, with a first-person ending on both nouns. The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 7:16 prints בֵּיתְךָ וּמַמְלַכְתְּךָ, “your house, your kingdom”, with a second-person ending. Brenton’s Greek of 1 Chronicles 17:14 changes the second to “his kingdom” (αὐτοῦ), a third reading. The three texts name three different owners of the kingdom in the parallel promise.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
The two verses are the same promise in the same speech. In 1 Chronicles 17:14 the Lord speaks of the son as set in the Lord’s own house and kingdom (בְּבֵיתִי וּבְמַלְכוּתִי). In 2 Samuel 7:16 the Lord speaks to David of David’s own house and kingdom (בֵּיתְךָ וּמַמְלַכְתְּךָ). The house and the kingdom are the Lord’s in one book and David’s in the other.

original:
Preserved draft reasoning:
The Hebrew word names a shoot or sprout. The Greek word Ἀνατολή means a rising (of the sun or a star) and the East. Brenton’s English margin at this verse points to Luke 1:78. A reader can therefore set the KJV’s plant image beside the Greek’s rising image for the same servant.

Additional retained draft evidence/qualification:
The Hebrew word מוֹפֵת means a sign or wonder (the KJV margin has “of wonder, or, sign”). The Greek compound τερατοσκόποι is built from “portent” and “watch”, and Brenton’s English renders it “diviners”. A reader of the KJV has companions who are themselves a sign; a reader of the Greek has companions who watch portents.

Both translators treat the word as a title or name.
